guide.title: Protein supplements: total intake, training and label quality
guide.summary: A powder is one way to supply dietary protein. The useful comparison starts with actual protein content and the training context.
guide.evidence: Trial syntheses support modest additional gains when protein supplementation accompanies resistance training. The benefit depends on the wider diet and training programme.
guide.limitations: Trials do not establish that every whey, plant or fermented product has the same effect. A price ranking is not a ranking of digestibility, amino-acid quality or clinical benefit.
guide.catalogReading: Use cost per gram of labelled protein rather than cost per gram of powder. Check serving size, concentration, ingredient source and label evidence separately.
guide.safety: Check food allergens and individual dietary restrictions. People with medically restricted protein intake need individual advice.
guide.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Stomach and intestinal enzymes break dietary protein into smaller peptides and amino acids.
The small intestine absorbs these building blocks into circulation.
Tissues use amino acids to make proteins; resistance training provides a stimulus for muscle adaptation.
guide.treatment: Protein supplementation can help address inadequate intake within a nutrition plan. Powder alone does not cure muscle wasting or an illness causing poor nutrition.
guide.whoMayBenefit: People unable to meet assessed protein needs through food, including some athletes or people receiving supervised nutritional care.
guide.routineUse: Everyone needs dietary protein; everyone does not need protein powder. Reassess the food gap rather than assuming lifelong use.

whoCanConsider: Adults whose food intake leaves a protein gap, including people with higher requirements from training.
People who find an appropriate powder more practical than adding another protein-containing meal.
whoShouldReview: Kidney disease or an existing protein-restricted diet requires an individualized nutrition plan.
Milk, egg, soy or other food allergy requires ingredient and allergen review; whey is milk-derived.
buyingGuide.foodSummary: Food can supply protein without a powder. Judge the need from total intake, preferences and practical meal choices.

dos.title: Count food first
dos.detail: Check whether your normal meals leave an assessed protein gap before paying for a powder.

dos.title: Compare actual protein
dos.detail: Use labelled protein per serving and cost per gram of protein; check the source and allergens.

donts.title: Don't count powder as protein
donts.detail: A scoop's full weight includes ingredients beyond protein; compare the declared concentration and serving size.

donts.title: Don't buy more automatically
donts.detail: Extra powder has low purchase priority when food already meets your needs or it displaces necessary meals.

intakeGuide.summary: Assess total daily protein from food first; powder only fills a genuine gap.

pathway.title: From dietary protein to tissue proteins
pathway.summary: Protein is digested into smaller building blocks before tissues can use it. The powder itself does not travel intact to muscle.

steps.label: Food proteins enter the stomach
steps.detail: Stomach acid and enzymes begin breaking down proteins from food or supplements.

steps.label: Enzymes release smaller building blocks
steps.detail: Pancreatic and intestinal enzymes continue digestion into peptides and amino acids.

steps.label: Absorbed amino acids enter circulation
steps.detail: The intestinal lining absorbs the digested building blocks; blood distributes amino acids to tissues.

steps.label: Cells assemble their own proteins
steps.detail: Tissues use amino acids for ongoing protein turnover; resistance exercise stimulates muscle protein synthesis.

pathway.caveat: This is normal protein metabolism. More powder does not guarantee more muscle when total intake and training already meet needs.
